title: A novel mRNA-based multi-epitope vaccine for rabies virus computationally designed via reverse vaccinology and immunoinformatics - Scientific Reports
content: Researchers have developed a novel mRNA-based multi-epitope vaccine for the rabies virus using computational approaches. The vaccine was designed to target multiple epitopes of the virus, including CTL and HTL epitopes, and was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, non-toxic, and immunogenic. The vaccine construct was optimized for codon usage and was predicted to have a high expression level in the human host. The researchers used various computational tools to predict the binding affinity of the vaccine with target immune cell receptors, including TLR4, and to evaluate the dynamic behavior and stability of the docked complex. The results suggest that the vaccine has the potential to trigger a strong immune response against the rabies virus. The researchers also performed an in silico immune simulation to evaluate the potential of the vaccine to trigger the host immune system. The simulation results suggest that the vaccine can induce a strong immune response and provide protection against the rabies virus. The researchers conclude that the developed vaccine has the potential to be a promising candidate for the prevention of rabies.

title: Salmonella nedir? Gıda zehirlenmesine karşı aşı geliştiriliyor
content: A team of scientists from the University of Maryland is developing a vaccine against Salmonella, a major cause of foodborne illness, with promising early results. The vaccine, called TSCV (Trivalent Salmonella Conjugate Vaccine), targets three distinct Salmonella serovars: Salmonella Typhi, which causes typhoid fever, and two others known to cause severe infections in children. In Phase 1 clinical trials involving 22 healthy adult volunteers in the U.S., the vaccine was found to be safe, well-tolerated, and effective in triggering a strong immune response, with the only reported side effect being mild pain at the injection site. According to co-author Prof. Myron Levine, 'These findings establish a strong foundation for future studies.' Salmonella infections, which commonly stem from undercooked meat, poultry, eggs, or unwashed produce—and occasionally from person-to-person contact—cause over 1 million cases annually in the U.S., leading to thousands of hospitalizations. The disease poses a significant risk to young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The study's small scale does not diminish its significance, as the results indicate substantial potential for TSCV to become a vital preventive tool, particularly in regions where children are most vulnerable.

title: SPIKEVAX (covid-19 vaccine, mrna) injection, suspension [Moderna US, Inc.]
content: The article reports on the safety and reactogenicity data from several Phase 2/3 studies of Moderna’s SPIKEVAX COVID‑19 vaccine (original monovalent and bivalent formulations).  In the largest study (Study 1), 30,346 adults aged 18 + were randomized to receive two 100 µg doses of SPIKEVAX (n = 15,184) or placebo (n = 15,162).  The cohort had a median age of 52 years, 75.2 % were 18‑64 years and 24.8 % were 65 + , and 52.6 % were male.  Solicited local and systemic adverse reactions were more common after vaccine than placebo, with pain at the injection site reported in up to 76.3 % of 65‑year‑olds and fatigue in 58.1 %.  Unsolicited adverse events occurred in 31.3 % of vaccine recipients versus 28.6 % of placebo recipients; lymphadenopathy was reported by 1.7 % of vaccine versus 0.8 % of placebo recipients.  Serious adverse events were 1.8 % in the vaccine group and 1.9 % in the placebo group, with no clear causal link to the vaccine.  In Study 2, 198 adults received two 100 µg doses followed by a 50 µg booster; solicited reactions after the booster included pain (86 %) and fatigue (62 %).  No serious adverse events were reported after the booster.  A large booster cohort (19,609 participants) received a single 50 µg dose; 31.7 % reported unsolicited events and 0.5 % had serious adverse events, none deemed vaccine‑related.  In a bivalent booster comparison (Study 5), 511 participants received a 50 µg Moderna bivalent booster and 376 received a 50 µg SPIKEVAX booster; serious adverse events were 0.6 % and 2.7 % respectively, with no events considered related to the vaccine.  In adolescents (12‑17 years, Study 3), 3,726 participants were enrolled (2,486 vaccine, 1,240 placebo); solicited reactions were more frequent in the vaccine arm, and no serious adverse events were reported.  Overall, the data indicate that SPIKEVAX is generally well tolerated, with reactogenicity rates consistent with other mRNA COVID‑19 vaccines and no new safety signals identified.

title: Nasal vaccines and the future of immunization
content: Nasals vaccines avoid needles and can trigger mucosal immunity at the infection site, offering potential to curb transmission. In the U.S., FluMist, a live‑attenuated influenza vaccine, is the only FDA‑approved nasal vaccine, available since 2003 and approved for at‑home use in the 2025‑2026 flu season (source). Other candidates target RSV, H5N1, and SARS‑CoV‑2. Nasal COVID‑19 vaccines have received emergency licenses in India, Russia, China, and Iran, and several are in preclinical or clinical stages. A hamster study using a chimpanzee adenovirus vector showed that nasal immunization prevented sequential viral transmission to unvaccinated hamsters (source). A phase‑1 trial of CVXGA1, a PIV5‑based vaccine, elicited mucosal and systemic responses in 12‑53‑year‑olds, and a phase‑2b trial is underway (source). Nanogel‑based RSV vaccine prevented viral invasion in both upper and lower respiratory tracts in rats (source). Challenges include mucosal barriers (mucus, cilia, secretions), tolerance of the mucosal immune system, and potential for adjuvants to reach the brain, as illustrated by the 2000 Swiss FluMist withdrawal after facial palsy cases linked to an E. coli enterotoxin adjuvant (source). Pre‑existing immunity can blunt FluMist efficacy, and effectiveness varies by age and strain match (source). Advances involve diverse vectors, mRNA, adjuvants, and delivery systems such as polymeric nanogels that adhere to mucosa and release antigen (source). A prime‑and‑boost strategy—intramuscular prime followed by nasal boost—may enhance mucosal defenses against SARS‑CoV‑2 and other respiratory pathogens (source). The future depends on regulatory approval and sustained funding; recent stop‑work orders and grant suspensions threaten clinical development (source).

title: SK바이오사이언스, 자체 개발 수두백신 1회→2회 접종 위한 임상 3상 나선다
content: SK BioScience has submitted a global Phase 3 IND to the Korean Food and Drug Administration for its own varicella vaccine, SkyBarisella, to evaluate a second‑dose (2‑dose) schedule. The trial will enroll about 800 children aged 12 months to 12 years, administer two doses, and assess immunogenicity and safety, with completion targeted for 2027. SkyBarisella was launched in Korea in 2018, received WHO pre‑qualification (PQ) in 2019, and has already been administered to more than 5 million people worldwide. The company has secured a long‑term supply contract with PAHO for 2025‑2027 and plans to accelerate its entry into the global varicella market. WHO’s SAGE officially recommended a 2‑dose schedule in March 2023, and countries such as the United States (since 2006), Germany, and Japan have adopted it, reducing varicella incidence by over 85 %. Market research by Global Market Insights projects the global varicella vaccine market to grow from about US$3.4 billion in 2024 to US$6.3 billion in 2034, a CAGR of 6.5 %. SK BioScience’s development head said, '수두백신 2도즈는 WHO PQ 기반 국제 조달 경험과 R&D 성과를 바탕으로 빠르게 개발을 진행하는 전략적 파이프라인' and added, '생산 안정성과 우수한 면역원성을 기반으로 단기간에 개발을 완료하고 글로벌 시장에서 경쟁하겠다'.

title: Scientists Create Heat-Proof Rabies Shot That Works in One Dose
content: Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder have created a heat‑stable rabies vaccine that can survive up to 104 °F for at least three months and elicits an immune response nearly ten times stronger than the conventional multi‑dose liquid vaccine, according to a study published in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences. The vaccine is produced by spray‑drying inactivated rabies virus into sugar‑based microparticles that are then coated with a nanoscopic layer of aluminum oxide—'sapphire'—using atomic layer deposition. The coating dissolves slowly after injection, releasing the antigen over days or weeks. In mouse studies, a single injection of the coated particles produced a stronger immune response than five doses of the standard vaccine. Professor Ted Randolph, who led the research, said, 'The proteins basically want to make cheese. You have to keep them from making cheese for long enough that you can manufacture the vaccines, get them to pharmacies and hospitals, and get them to patients.' The formulation could be transported without refrigeration, making it suitable for rural areas in India, Africa, and other developing regions where 60,000 people die from rabies each year. Randolph and colleague Robert Garcea have founded VitriVax to commercialize the technology, with human trials expected in at least two years. "You can now take these vaccines to places without refrigeration, and even to places that get hot," Randolph added, "so transportation through rural India or wherever you're going is no longer a problem."

title: Impfung verhinderte 10.000 Erkrankungen
content: A study by experts from the Medical University of Vienna, published in the journal 'Vaccine', analyzed lab-confirmed cases of tick-borne encephalitis (FSME) in Austria from 2000 to 2024. The findings indicate that the FSME vaccination prevented more than 10,000 hospitalizations, over 4,000 severe cases, and 80 deaths during this period. The study evaluated 2,260 hospitalizations due to FSME, with adults aged 16–59 most affected, followed by those over 60; 12% of cases involved children under 15. Among hospitalized patients, 1,000 experienced severe disease courses, and 26 (1.2%) died. No causal treatment exists for FSME, which can lead to serious neurological long-term effects. The study confirms that consistent vaccination offers approximately 99% protection, while irregular but ongoing booster doses provide over 90% protection. Despite high vaccination rates in Austria—among the highest in Europe—the proportion of people receiving recommended vaccinations has declined over time. This trend coincides with a significant rise in FSME cases among under- or non-vaccinated individuals. The researchers emphasize that sustained high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent further increases in cases and to significantly reduce the burden on Austria’s healthcare system.

title: "Effetti avversi", Chikungunya: stop al vaccino Ixchiq
content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) suspended the license of the chikungunya vaccine Ixchiq, produced by Valneva, on 25 August 2025. The decision followed reports of four new serious adverse events, three involving people aged 70‑82, recorded in the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). The suspension triggered a sharp market reaction: Valneva shares fell 26.07 % at the Paris Bourse, dropping to 3.73 € per share after a low of 3.566 €. Ixchiq had been approved by the FDA in November 2023 and is one of only two U.S. vaccines against chikungunya. The World Health Organization (WHO) had issued an alert in July 2025 after detecting epidemic‑like signals, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) reported 27 outbreaks in Europe that year. Valneva’s CEO, Thomas Lingelbach, said, 'While we evaluate the next steps, and with the clear threat of chikungunya continuing to grow globally, Valneva remains fully committed to maintaining access to our vaccine as a global health tool to address and prevent outbreaks of this devastating disease.' The company has not altered its revenue forecasts but is assessing the financial impact of a possible permanent U.S. withdrawal. Chikungunya, which originated in East Africa in the 1950s, has spread to over 110 countries; between 2013 and 2023, more than 3.7 million cases were reported in the Americas. The vaccine’s adverse event history includes 17 serious events, including two deaths, in people aged 62‑89, which led to a temporary pause for those over 60 in August 2025.
